## 3. **Since the work requires actual model training on this unsupervised signal, simply the accuracy of the pseudo label does not suffice (as in Fig 3b). Unclear if the original test set (ground truth labels) is biased towards getting correctness right, or are we measuring the how often the consistency indicator lines up with correct or incorrect prediction. It would be prudent to report F1, or correlation between the metrics and the binary ground truth by Spearman or Somer's D correlation as done in https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04109.**
We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. To address this, we expanded our evaluation on Qwen-4B-Base to include **F1 Score** and **Spearman’s Rank Correlation following your suggestions,**

We analyzed performance across four subsets of problem difficulty: (1) **Confident Correct (where the original model’s** majority answer ≥ N/2 votes is correct **)**, (2) **Confident Incorrect (where the original model’s** majority answer ≥ N/2 votes is **incorrect )**, (3) **Not Confident Correct (where the original model’s** majority answer < N/2 votes is **correct )**, and (4) **Not Confident Incorrect**.
| Method/Qwen-4B-Base/Average Pass@1 over 16 rollouts | confident correct datasets | confident incorrect datasets | not confident correct datasets | not confident incorrect datasets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| harmonic(Self-Harmony) | **99.61** | **77.73** | **93.28** | **61.25** |
| TTRL(Majority Voting) | 98.90 | 76.81 | 92.35 | 58.97 |

| Method/Qwen-4B-Base/F1 | confident correct datasets | confident incorrect datasets | not confident correct datasets | not confident incorrect datasets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| harmonic(Self-Harmony) | **99.35** | **75.76** | **93.07** | **66.43** |
| TTRL(Majority Voting) | 88.89 | 69.87 | 91.26 | 63.41 |

Self-Harmony achieves significantly higher F1 scores across all subsets. Most notably, in the "Confident Correct" setting, Self-Harmony improves F1 by over 10 points (99.35 vs. 88.89). This indicates that our Harmonic Mean Score (HMS) is far more effective at correctly identifying and retrieving valid training signals without discarding them (high recall) or accepting noise (high precision).

| Method/Qwen-4B-Base/Spearman $\rho$(%) | confident correct datasets | confident incorrect datasets | not confident correct datasets | not confident incorrect datasets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| harmonic(Self-Harmony) | 18.35 | **36.51** | **37.16** | **30.11** |
| TTRL(Majority Voting) | **35.82** | 15.19 | 35.83 | 29.34 |

The most critical finding lies in the Confident Incorrect subset. Here, Majority Voting exhibits a very low correlation (15.19), confirming that when the model hallucinates confidently, vote counts become decoupled from correctness. In contrast, Self-Harmony maintains a much stronger correlation (36.51).  

Regarding the Confident–Correct subset, the relatively lower Spearman correlation of Self-Harmony should not be interpreted as reduced pseudo-label quality. Rather, Self-Harmony produces near-perfect consistency in this regime (F1 ≈ 1), leaving very little variability for rank-based correlation metrics to detect. Thus, the drop reflects a statistical ceiling effect rather than a failure of the method.

These results confirm that **HMS successfully penalizes "confident hallucinations" (view-dependent errors)**. Even when the model is confidently wrong, the lower harmonic mean score (due to inconsistency across views) better reflects the low probability of correctness, providing a safer and more aligned training signal than majority voting.

We thank Reviewer for the positive assessment of our work, specifically regarding the soundness of the intuition and the comprehensive nature of our experiments. We particularly appreciate the insightful suggestion to analyze performance based on confidence and correctness categories. We have performed this analysis, and the results further validate the robustness of Self-Harmony.

summary.value: This paper presents "self-harmony" an alternative to final-response consistency like self-consistency often used for test time scaling and more importantly for unsupervised supervision at test time. While self-consistency involves temperature sampling multiple solutions and selecting the one corresponding to the majority answer, the authors propose looking at the same problem from "multiple views" done by creating multiple rephrasings of the input query and selecting the answer consistent across these views by using the harmonic mean. The model is then trained on this unsupervised signal and the performance is reported. The authors argue that self-harmony is useful even in cases when self-consistency fails, i.e., model consistently arriving at the wrong answer.

strengths.value:
- Obtaining unsupervised signals for improving reasoning performance is an important area of work with potential applications in scaling reasoning performance during pretraining or in the wild, where annotations are not available. This paper makes a contribution towards the broader goal.
- The paper is well-structured and easy-to-follow with decent empirical gains in the main resutls as well as some theoretical justifications for the view-invariant info-max objective.

## 6. **Similarly, with fixed λ, what happens if one considers more than two views? For instance, when K > 2, does multiple views lead to the general form of the harmonic mean? What might be the impact of having more views? At least from theoretical viewpoint, more (diverse) views should give better and better performance, although there is a possibility of plateauing over certain threshold.**
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. You have correctly identified a natural extension of our theoretical framework.

### Generalization to Multiple Views (K > 2)

You asked if considering more than two views leads to the general form of the harmonic mean. The answer is **yes** as well.

We have derived the extension of Theorem 3.1 for K views. Following the same logic as our proof for K=2, we assume X is uniformly distributed over K views {$x_1, …, x_k$}. Let $\bar{p}(a)$ be the arithmetic mean and σ²(a) be the variance across views:

$$
p̄(a) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} p(a|x_k)
$$

$$
σ²(a) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} (p(a|x_k) - \bar{p}(a))²
$$

Using the second-order Taylor expansion of the KL-divergence, the mutual information term generalizes to the variance:

$$
I(Z_a; X) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathrm{KL}(p_k \| \bar{p}) \approx \frac{σ²(a)}{2\bar{p}(a)(1-\bar{p}(a))}
$$

Applying the same simplification as the main proof (approximating the denominator 1-\bar{p} ≈ 1), our objective with λ=2 becomes:

$$
J_2(a) \approx \bar{p}(a) - \frac{σ^2(a)}{\bar{p}(a)}
$$

Separately, if we take the **Generalized Harmonic Mean** of K views, and perform a Taylor expansion around the arithmetic mean p̄, we obtain the exact same form:

$$
H_K(a) = \left(\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} p(a|x_k)^{-1}\right)^{-1}
$$

$$
H_K(a) \approx \bar{p}(a) - \frac{σ²(a)}{\bar{p}(a)}
$$

Thus, maximizing the invariant Infomax objective with λ=2 for K views is theoretically equivalent to maximizing the Generalized Honic Mean. 

### Impact of More Views and Plateauing

Regarding the impact of increasing K, we agree with your hypothesis:

• **Performance:** Theoretically, increasing K provides a better estimate of the "true" probability by reducing the variance of the estimator, leading to better separation between correct and incorrect pseudolabels.

• **Plateauing:** In practice, performance plateaus because generating K *diverse* (independent) views becomes increasingly difficult. As views become correlated (e.g., similar prompts yielding similar logits), the marginal gain in Mutual Information diminishes. Furthermore, if additional views are of lower quality (high noise), they may degrade the consensus.




## 7. **Follow-up question: If it is possible, I wonder what the impact of the second-order approximation is. Yes, computationally, having a closed-form solution is hugely beneficial, but the second-order approximation of the KL is tight only when the two probabilities are quite similar. Thus, if one puts in enough budget, I wonder if maximizing the infomax objective directly (with an appropriate KL estimator) gives better pseudo-label, and thus better performance. Or, whether the performance gain is minimal and the approximation objective is good as it is.**

To evaluate whether the second-order approximation limits performance, we implemented a KL-based estimator and optimized the full Infomax objective without approximation. Specifically, we replaced our quadratic surrogate with the divergence term.
$g(p)=\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\mathrm{Bern}(p)\,\Vert\,\mathrm{Bern}(q)\bigr)
=p\ln\frac{p}{q}+(1-p)\ln\frac{1-p}{1-q}$
and compared the resulting pseudo-labels against Self-Harmony. The evaluation metric is mean pass@1 across 16 rollouts, stratified into the four difficulty subsets:

| Qwen3-4B-Base | confident correct dataset | confident incorrect dataset | not confident correct dataset | not confident incorrect dataset|
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| harmonic(Self-Harmony) | **99.61** | **77.73** | **93.28** | **61.25** |
| full infomax | 99.22 | 75.78 | 90.10 | 60.00 |

Directly optimizing the full Infomax objective does not improve over the second-order approximation; in fact, Self-Harmony achieves the highest performance in all subsets. Since Self-Harmony corresponds to the second-order approximation of the Infomax objective, this indicates that the approximation is not only computationally efficient but also advantageous in practice. The second-order formulation naturally suppresses such high-order fluctuations, preventing the fitting of high-order noise while still rewarding consistency across paraphrased views.

## **1. Consensus Strengths**
1. Dominant Empirical Performance — All reviewers (v4TH, dk94, 962B, RRhh) acknowledged that Self-Harmony delivers superior results. Reviewer dk94 emphasized that the method ranks “1st in 28 of 30 settings” across six major reasoning benchmarks and five models in two model families.

3. Intuitive & Elegant Framework — The Dual-Role (Solver + Reframer) architecture was praised as “elegant, practical, and scalable” (dk94), “clear and solid” (v4TH), and important for enabling unsupervised signals in the wild (RRhh).
4. Robustness & Reproducibility — Reviewers noted the training stability (dk94) and robustness to hyperparameters (962B). v4TH praised the release of reproducible code.
5. High Quality of Presentation — dk94 highlighted that the paper “stands out for its clarity,” v4TH called it “well-written,” and RRhh described it as “well-structured and easy-to-follow.”

## **2. Factual Resolution of Major Technical Concerns**

Only the major issues are summarized below:

### Concern: What drives the gains beyond standard Self-Consistency / Majority Voting? (RRhh, 962B)

Evidence:
- Analytical Decomposition:
        $\text{HMS} = \frac{1}{2} \biggl[ \underbrace{{(p_{0}(a) + p_{1}(a))}}\_{\text{Self Consistency}} - \underbrace{{\frac{(p_{0}(a) - p_{1}(a))^2}{p_{0}(a) + p_{1}(a)}}}\_{\text{View Invariance}}\biggl]$. Self-Harmony suppresses answers that are confident but fragile.
        
- Universal Gains across Quadrants: The trained model improves Mean Pass@1 across all four quadrant subsets (confident-correct, confident-incorrect, not-confident-correct, not-confident-incorrect) — demonstrating benefits without trade-offs.
- Cleaner Training Signal (Correlation): On the Confident-Incorrect subset, Majority Voting produces noisy pseudo-labels (Spearman = 15.19%), whereas Self-Harmony provides a significantly stronger signal (Spearman = 36.51%).
- Inference-Only Utility: Even without training, Self-Harmony yields higher Pass@1 than Majority Voting across models (4B, 8B), rollout budgets (32–256), and all quadrant subsets.

Resolution: Self-Harmony enhances performance on both easy and hard subsets, with the largest gains occurring where Majority Voting fails, in both inference-only and training regimes.

### Concern:  What intuition and evidence support self-harmony's advantage over other aggregator? (v4TH, RRhh)
Evidence: 
- A direct comparison against Arithmetic, Geometric, Quadratic Mean, and Infomax without second-order approximation

Resolution: Self-Harmony is consistently the strongest across all quadrants.
### Concern: Does paraphrasing drift from the Reframer incorrectly down-weight valid answers? (dk94)
Evidence: 
- Sensitivity analysis varying both Reframer sizes (0.6B → 14B) and Solver sizes (1.7B → 8B) shows consistently large improvements over the baseline solver (before training) across all configurations. Even with a noisy 0.6B Reframer, the Confident-Correct subset improves sharply (like Qwen-4B: 83.98% → 96.48% in Mean Pass@1 under 16 rollouts).

Resolution: Self-Harmony does not penalize valid solutions under semantic drift and remains effective without requiring a strong Reframer.
### Concern: Can the theoretical framework be generalized? (v4TH)
Evidence:
- We show that introducing a tunable λ recovers different Generalized Means under second-order approximation.
- Theorem 3.1 was further extended to support multi-view and non-uniform prior assumptions.

Resolution: These theoretical extensions confirm that the framework is not restricted to the original two-view, uniform-prior, λ = 2 setting.

---
To conclude, we hope the following four points are helpful for the final decision:
1. State-of-the-art results in label-free test-time RL without external reward models.
2. A new pseudo-label selector that consistently outperforms majority voting in both inference-only and training settings.
3. Theoretical justification, grounding the method in Infomax with second-order extensions.
4. A simple and robust dual-role architecture that scales across models and reframer qualities, enabling stable label-free improvement of LLMs.

## 2. **How sensitive is the performance to small perturbations in the paraphrased questions or to imperfect semantic equivalence?  target on “introducing small wording biases or contextual cues—the harmonic mean could incorrectly down-weight valid answers”**

We appreciate this insightful concern. The reviewer identifies a potential risk: if the paraphrasing step introduces semantic drift or wording biases, the strict Harmonic Mean criterion might incorrectly down-weight valid answers.

To quantify this risk, we conducted a safety stress test with the Confident Correct subset of the dataset. On this subset, the Initial Model has a high baseline reliability (Mean Pass@1 $\approx$ 84-89%). If semantic drift were a major issue, the Harmonic Mean would punish these valid answers, causing the mean Pass@1 score in 16 rollouts to drop. **To simulate imperfect semantic equivalence, we utilized model scale as a proxy for paraphrase quality**. We tested Solvers of varying sizes paired with Reframers ranging from a tiny 0.6B (high noise/perturbation) to 14B.

| Self-Harmony/confident correct datasets | Baseline | Ours with 0.6b-reframer | Ours with 1.7b-reframer | Ours with 4b-reframer | Ours with 14b-reframer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-1.7B-Base | 86.32 | 94.92 | 94.92 | 95.31 | 96.48 |
| Qwen3-4B-Base | 83.98 | 96.48 | 97.65 | 98.04 | 98.36 |
| Qwen3-8B-Base | 89.06 | 97.85 | 97.75 | 98.02 | 99.07 |

- Robustness to Semantic Drift: Even when using a 0.6B Reframer which generates lower-fidelity paraphrases and introduces significant wording bias, we observe massive gains in Mean Pass@1 over the Initial Model (like Qwen-4B improves from 83.98% $\to$ 96.48%). This confirms that the Harmonic Mean is not overly sensitive to perturbations; it successfully identifies consistency even when the rephrasing is noisy, without discarding valid answers.
- Effectiveness on Small Models: Addressing the concern regarding the "self-contained" assumption for smaller models, our method functions exceptionally well even with a 1.7B Solver (86.32% $\to$ 94.92%). This contradicts the worry that high linguistic competence is a strict prerequisite; the method is robust across model scales.

We hope these additional experiments could provide sufficient clarity to reviewer's concern, and we would be grateful to know if there are any remaining questions we can further clarify. We look forward to continuing the discussion.

We sincerely thank Reviewer for exceptionally positive and constructive review, and for the high rating of 8 (accept). We are delighted that they found our paper "well-written," with "clear and solid intuition," "theoretically well-grounded," and supported by "extensive experiments."

Their thoughtful questions and suggestions are invaluable, and we will incorporate them to strengthen the revision. We address each point below.

## 1. **The authors mention that the reward design plays a role in obtaninig SOTA performance (Section 4.3), but the only mention of how the weights involved with the rewards are set $(w_f, w_d)$ is in Appendix E.4, mentioned in the passing only "weights set to match the proportional influence ...". This design choice should sufficiently be elaborated as well.**

We wish to clarify that the weights for the additive baseline were not chosen arbitrarily; they were mathematically derived to ensure a rigorous and fair comparison with our multiplicative design. Specifically, we aligned the weights based on the effective gradients derived from a first-order Taylor expansion.

Our multiplicative reward is defined as:
$$R_{\text{mult}} = (1 - w_f R_f)(1 - w_d R_d)R_{\text{solve}}$$
For correct answers ($R_{\text{solve}}=1$) and small penalty terms, this linearizes to:
$$R_{\text{mult}} \approx R_{\text{solve}} - w_f R_f - w_d R_d$$
To control for hyperparameter influence, we configured the additive baseline ($R_{\text{add}} = w_3 R_{\text{solve}} + w_1 R_f + w_2 R_d$) to match this approximation strictly:
$$w_3 = 1, w_1 = -w_f, w_2 = -w_d$$

This alignment ensures that both models are subject to identical penalty magnitudes for format and diversity violations. Consequently, the superior performance of Self-Harmony can be attributed to the structural advantage of the multiplicative design (which acts as a strict "AND" gate) rather than disparate hyperparameter settings. 
    
## 2. **Although there isn't anything (significantly) wrong with the theoretical discussions, I believe there are some parts that warrant further discussion:**
-  **I think it is beneficial to explicitly state the "second-order approximation" in the main text for the camera-ready version.**

    Thank you for pointing out. We’ve updated second-order approximation in revision already.

- **The assumption that the view random variable is uniform is implicit and made explicitly only in the proof. This should be made clear in the main text.**

    Thank you for pointing out. We’ve updated approximation in revision already.

## 3. **Is there any connection between the core intuition here and group-invariant learning[1] or invariant risk minimization[2]? I don't recall any discussions relating to this line of works in the paper.**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. Our approach is indeed conceptually related to group-invariant learning [1] and invariant risk minimization (IRM) [2], and we made this connection explicit in the revision.

Relation to group-invariant learning.

Paraphrased questions can be interpreted as task-specific transformations that preserve semantic meaning. Assumption 3.1 states that correctness of the true answer is approximately invariant under these transformations, whereas spurious answers are view-dependent. While we do not build a group-equivariant architecture in the strict sense of [1], the View-Invariant Infomax objective operationalizes a similar invariance principle—applied at the level of answers under paraphrased views rather than features under group actions. 

Relation to IRM.

IRM enforces predictors that perform optimally across multiple environments. In our setting, paraphrased views $X \in \{x, x'\}$ serve as environments, and Assumption 3.1 posits that only the true answer remains environment-invariant. The objective
$J_\lambda(a) = I(Z_a; A) - \lambda\, I(Z_a; X)$ maximizes correctness while penalizing dependence on view-specific information, mirroring the IRM constraint but at test-time pseudo-label selection rather than representation learning during supervised training.

We appreciate the reviewer for highlighting this theoretical angle; it helped us better position our contribution within the broader invariance literature.

summary.value: This paper proposes Self-Harmony, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) framework that improves reasoning stability without external supervision. The key idea is that a correct answer should remain consistent across both an original question and its paraphrase. A single model plays two cooperative roles: a Solver that answers and a Reframer that rephrases the question to provide a second view. Pseudo-labels are then chosen using the harmonic mean of answer frequencies from both views, emphasizing solutions robust to rewording while down-weighting view-specific errors. The authors provide theoretical justification for this criterion and integrate it into a self-play reinforcement loop. Across five reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, AIME24, GPQA, MMLU-Pro) and five open-source models, Self-Harmony achieves new state-of-the-art results—ranking first in 28 of 30 settings—and demonstrates superior training stability and pseudo-label accuracy.

strengths.value:
This paper stands out for its clarity and strong empirical results. The idea of enforcing consistency across paraphrased versions of a question is simple yet powerful—it directly targets a core weakness of existing test-time RL methods that overfit to their own biases. Using a single model in dual roles (Solver and Reframer) is elegant and avoids the need for extra models or supervision, making the approach practical and scalable. The harmonic mean pseudo-label rule is theoretically grounded and nicely bridges information-theoretic reasoning with an intuitive motivation. 

The experiments are extensive and convincing: strong gains across five benchmarks, stable training curves, and robustness across model sizes all strengthen the paper’s credibility. Overall, Self-Harmony feels like a solid, well-executed contribution that advances test-time adaptation in a meaningful and reproducible way.

weaknesses.value:
The harmonic mean rule, while supported by a theoretical derivation, still feels somewhat heuristic in how it’s applied. In practice, the paper does not deeply analyze why the harmonic mean performs better than simpler alternatives like averaging or weighted voting, or under what conditions it might fail. For instance, if the paraphrasing step inadvertently shifts the semantics of the question—introducing small wording biases or contextual cues—the harmonic mean could incorrectly down-weight valid answers. A sensitivity analysis or qualitative study of such “semantic drift” cases would make the claim of robustness more convincing.

Finally, the “self-contained” assumption might break for smaller or less instruction-tuned models, since paraphrasing quality heavily depends on the model’s own linguistic competence—an issue not fully explored in the experiments.

## 4. **(Minor) Are there any literature from human psychology or education for the claim "common human robustness heuristic: when confronted with uncertainty, people often check solutions ..." (line 161)?**

The reviewer is correct that the intuition has precedents in human psychology and education.

(i) Polya’s problem-solving heuristics. In How to Solve It (Polya, 1945), one of the core verification strategies is: “Can you obtain the result differently?” — i.e., when a solver is uncertain, they intentionally reformulate the problem to validate the answer from another perspective. This directly aligns with our mechanism of reframing under uncertainty.

(ii) Cognitive Flexibility Theory. Spiro et al. (1988, 1992) show that in ill-structured problems, reasoning through multiple representations and revisiting content from alternative perspectives enables more robust judgments than relying on a single formulation. While originally framed for learning rather than answer verification, it supports the broader psychological intuition that multiple perspectives help mitigate uncertainty.

We cite these work in revision already.

## 5. **What happens if is also tunable? In other words, under two views, would one still be able to derive Eqn. (1) as a function of ? If that is the case, then what is the impact of tuning across various values?**
    
We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. We confirm that **yes**, Eqn. (1) can be derived as a function of an arbitrary λ, and doing so reveals a fascinating connection between the Invariant Infomax objective and the family of Generalized Means.
    
### 1. Deriving the General Form
    
Following the proof in Appendix A (specifically Eq. 13 and 14), we derived the second-order Taylor approximation for the view-consistency term:
    
$$
I(Z_a; X) \approx \frac{\delta(a)^2}{2\bar{p}(a)}
$$
    
If we leave λ as a free parameter in the objective $J_λ(a) = I(Z_a; A) - λ I(Z_a; X)$, the objective approximates to:
    
$$
J_\lambda(a) \approx \bar{p}(a) - \lambda \frac{\delta(a)^2}{2\bar{p}(a)}
$$
    
### 2. Connection to Generalized Means
    
To understand the impact of tuning λ, we compare $J_λ(a)$ to the Taylor expansion of the Generalized Mean with exponent *k*, denoted as:
    
$$
M_k(p_0, p_1) = \left(\frac{p_0^k + p_1^k}{2}\right)^{1/k}
$$
    
The second-order expansion of $M_k$ around the mean $\bar{p}$ is known to be:
    
$$
M_k(p_0, p_1) \approx \bar{p}(a) + (k-1)\frac{\delta(a)^2}{2\bar{p}(a)}
$$
    
By equating the coefficients of the variance term in $J_λ$ and $M_k$, we find a direct mapping between the penalty weight λ and the power mean exponent *k*:

$$
-\frac{\lambda}{2} = \frac{k-1}{2} \quad \implies \quad k = 1 - \lambda
$$

### 3. Impact of Tuning λ

Tuning λ effectively changes which Pythagorean mean the objective maximizes. Increasing λ increases the penalty for disagreement between views (variance), making the selector more "conservative."

- **λ = -1 ⟹ k = 2 (Quadratic Mean/RMS):** The objective maximizes $\sqrt{(p_{0}^2 + p_{1}^2)/2}$. This effectively adds a bonus for variance ($\approx \bar{p} + \frac{\delta^2}{2\bar{p}}$). It is "risk-seeking": it rewards cases where views strongly disagree (high variance), which is generally undesirable for consistency checking.
- **λ = 0 ⟹ k = 1 (Arithmetic Mean):** The objective maximizes $\bar{p}(a)$. This corresponds to standard Majority Voting or mean-probability selection, which ignores view consistency entirely (coefficient of $\delta^2$ is 0).
- **λ = 1 ⟹ k = 0 (Geometric Mean):** The objective maximizes $\sqrt{p_{0}(a)p_{1}(a)}$. This balances confidence and consistency moderately.
- **λ = 2 ⟹ k = -1 (Harmonic Mean - Our Proposal):** As derived in Theorem 1, this maximizes $\frac{2p₀p₁}{p₀ + p₁}$. It penalizes variance with a coefficient of $-1$ ($\approx \bar{p} - \frac{\delta^2}{2\bar{p}}$).
- **λ → ∞ ⟹ k → -∞ (Minimum):** The objective approaches maximizing $min(p_0, p_1)$, the most conservative selection strategy.

With experiment showing below, the **harmonic mean is the best choice for pseudo label selector for our TTRL settings**. we evaluated the selectors on the Qwen3-4B-Base model. We categorized questions into four types based on model confidence (majority vote > N(number of rollouts)/2) and correctness(majority vote answer = ground truth).

| Qwen3-4B-Base | confident correct dataset | confident incorrect dataset | not confident correct dataset | not confident incorrect dataset|
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| arithmetic | 98.83 | 76.95 | 90.82 | 58.13 |
| harmonic(Self-Harmony) | **99.61** | **77.73** | **93.28** | **61.25** |
| quadratic | 98.43 | 76.25 | 89.61 | 60.98 |
| geometry | 99.22 | 76.17 | 91.23 | 58.89 |

## 8. **Also a follow-up: the authors consider uniform prior over the views. I wonder if one could be a bit more clever here, e.g., depending on the "persona" or the "strengths" of the current LLM, one could take that into account to make the prior non-uniform?**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. We utilized a uniform prior to model the "maximum entropy" scenario where the agent has no a priori knowledge of which view (or persona) is more reliable. This ensures the selector remains parameter-free and robust.
However, we agree that if one could estimate "persona strength" (e.g., via confidence scores), a non-uniform prior is the theoretically correct extension. One can indeed be "cleverer" by incorporating a prior $\pi \in (0,1)$ for the first view. This generalizes our theorem as follows:
- Weighted Marginal: The consensus probability becomes the weighted average $\bar{p}\_{\pi(a)} = \pi p\_{0}(a) + (1-\pi ) p\_{1}(a)$ 
- Weighted Penalty: The consistency term $I(Z_a;X)$ becomes a weighted sum of KL-divergences: $I(Z_a;X) = \pi KL(p\_0 \parallel \bar{p}\_{\pi}) + (1-\pi) KL(p\_1 \parallel \bar{p}\_{\pi})$ 
- Resulting Objective: Applying the second-order Taylor expansion yields a penalty proportional to the prior's variance $\pi(1-\pi)$. The resulting Weighted Invariant Score is: $S\_{\pi(a)} \approx \bar{p}\_{\pi(a)} - \frac{\pi(1-\pi)(p\_{0}(a) - p\_{1}(a))^2}{\bar{p}\_{\pi(a)}}$ 

This confirms the reviewer's intuition: if we identify a stronger persona (e.g., $\pi \to 1$), the variance term $\pi(1-\pi)$ shrinks, effectively relaxing the consistency constraint and allowing the stronger view to dominate.

## 9. **(Minor) As in many infomax papers (and as a theoretician myself), I wonder if this formulation of infomax (and its approximation) has been theoretically studied before, i.e., whether prior generalization bounds are applicable here (e.g., [3]). Or does this warrant further investigation for future work? If yes, which part of the new formulation yields novelty compared to prior literature?**
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and for pointing us towards Towards the Generalization of Multi-view Learning ([3]). And we really appreciate the connection drawn between our heuristic motivation and the formal generalization analysis in multi-view learning.
While both works draw inspiration from the general Information Maximization principle, there are fundamental differences in the problem setting, formulation, and application that distinguish our work from [3] and make their specific bounds not directly applicable, though highly relevant for future theoretical extensions.
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment and for highlighting the connection to Towards the Generalization of Multi-view Learning [3]. While both works build on the Infomax principle, the theoretical setting in [3] is not directly applicable to ours due to key differences in problem setup and formulation:

### 1. Different learning regimes.
[3] studies multi-view representation learning on static datasets, where views are fixed and sampled i.i.d. from a stationary distribution. In Self-Harmony, views are dynamically generated paraphrases during Test-Time RL, and the distribution of views changes as the Reframer policy adapts. This feedback loop breaks the i.i.d. assumption underlying the generalization bounds in [3].

### 2. Different Infomax objectives.
[3] uses Infomax to disentangle shared vs. private latent representations. In contrast, our View-Invariant Infomax is defined over pseudo-label selection: maximize $I(Z_a; A)$ while minimizing dependence on the view $I(Z_a; X)$. The goal is not to learn a latent space but to identify stable answers under paraphrase transformations.

### 3. Novel Approximation.
Our contribution is to convert this theoretical objective into a computationally efficient selector: the Harmonic Mean of answer frequencies. Unlike the entropic terms in [3], which require estimating complex mutual information, our proxy enables real-time scoring during inference.

We've added this citation in revision.

The reviewer is correct that the main focus of Liu et al. (2025b) is to compare prompting strategies.
However, we cited this paper specifically for its valuable formal definition of the exact failure mode of self-consistency that motivates Self-Harmony.
Our statement "...if p(Correct | x) < p(Wrong | x)..." is a direct, plain-English summary of what Liu et al. (2025b) formally define as a "hard question" (Definition 4.1). This is a case where the correct answer $a_{1}$ is not in the set of most probable answers ($\mathcal{S}$), meaning its probability is lower than that of the most-likely incorrect answer.
Crucially, Theorem 3 from Liu et al. (2025b) then proves the consequence: for these "hard questions," the probability of majority voting (SC) finding the correct answer approaches 0 as the number of samples increases.
This is the mathematical proof that majority voting "will amplify these spurious solutions."
Our paper is built to solve this exact, formally-defined problem. In the revision, we've made more discussion on this connection.

The Confident Incorrect result is particularly significant. These are cases where the model is "confidently wrong" (high majority consistency for an incorrect answer). Majority voting inevitably reinforces these errors. However, Self-Harmony achieves a higher Pass@1 (77.73% vs 76.81%), suggesting that the Harmonic Mean's dual-view constraint can better detect and recover from these high-confidence hallucinations than simple voting filters.

This baseline falls outside our problem setting. A "trained reward model" inherently requires a separate, labeled dataset for supervision. We do, however, compare against a "GT-Reward" (Table 1) as an oracle upper-bound, which is the strongest possible reward signal.

## 8. **Regarding 3(a), how often does the collapse happen and is it just on this specific dataset and/or model type? What are possible explanations or is it the entropy collapse seen in RLHF and how does the step where it happens relate to the size of the training set and the batch size?**
TTRL exhibits collapse only in the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model on the Math and MMLU-Pro datasets. There is entropy collapse, similar to the failure modes in RLHF. The model reward hacks the majority-vote pseudo-label: once biased toward a wrong answer, the majority signal reinforces that error, driving policy entropy to zero and locking the model into a deterministic, incorrect state. As for training step and batchsize, It happens in early stage of training (~20 steps) for both dataset while batchsize for Math is 128 and for MMLU-Pro is 32 respectively.

## 10. **(Minor) Very recently, there have been some issues regarding floating-point operations (https://x.com/QPHutu/status/1984258808332550245). Can the authors comment on whether this issue(?) applies to their experiments?**

The row MSE(fp16, bf16) reports, for each metric separately, the mean squared error between the fp16 and bf16 runs averaged across training steps. The differences are extremely small (2.02e-6, 1.53e-6, 2.63e-5), demonstrating that our training process and results are **stable across floating-point formats** and unaffected by the fp16 instability mentioned by the reviewer.

summary.value: The authors propose **Self-Harmony**, a new TTRL framework inspired by the Infomax principle. The core intuition is that the correct answer should appear consistently (robustly) across different versions of the question. The authors demonstrate that the argmax of the harmonic mean of the two probabilities under two different versions of the question approximately yields a good pseudo-label, and this is algorithmically achieved via appropriate prompt-engineered self-play. Its empirical efficacy is shown across various reasoning benchmarks and Qwen & Llama models, showing its superiority over prior TTRL approaches.

strengths.value:
- Well-written
- Clear and solid intuition
- Theoretically well-grounded
- Extensive experiments and benchmarks, as well as publicly released anonymized codes. Ablations provide a complete understanding of each component of the proposed algorithm and clearly show its superiority.

weaknesses.value:
- The authors mention that the reward design plays a role in obtaninig SOTA performance (Section 4.3), but the only mention of how the weights involved with the rewards are set ($w_f, w_d$) is in Appendix E.4, mentioned in the passing only "weights set to match the proportional influence ...". This design choice should sufficiently be elaborated as well.
- Although there isn't anything (significantly) wrong with the theoretical discussions, I believe there are some parts that warrant further discussion:
  - I think it is beneficial to explicitly state the "second-order approximation" in the main text for the camera-ready version.
  - The assumption that the view random variable $V$ is uniform is implicit and made explicitly only in the proof. This should be made clear in the main text.
  - The theory is only derived for two views and $\lambda = 2$ and uniform prior. I believe that more discussions on this would make the paper better; see Questions.

questions.value:
1. Is there any connection between the core intuition here and group-invariant learning [1] or invariant risk minimization [2]? I don't recall any discussions relating to this line of works in the paper.

2. (Minor) Are there any literature from human psychology or education for the claim "common human robustness heuristic: when confronted with uncertainty, people often check solutions ..." (line 161)?

3. What happens if $\lambda$ is also tunable? In other words, under two views, would one still be able to derive Eqn. (1) as a function of $\lambda$? If that is the case, then what is the impact of tuning $\lambda$ across various values?

4. Similarly, with fixed $\lambda$, what happens if one considers more than two views? For instance, when $\lambda = 2$, then does multiple views lead to the general form of the harmonic mean? What might be the impact of having more views? At least from theoretical viewpoint, more (diverse) views should give better and better performance, although there is a possibility of plateauing over certain threshold.

5. Follow-up question: If it is possible, I wonder what the impact of the second-order approximation is. Yes, computationally, having a closed-form solution is hugely beneficial, but the second-order approximation of the KL is tight only when the two probabilities are quite similar. Thus, if one puts in enough budget, I wonder if maximizing the infomax objective directly (with an appropriate KL estimator) gives better pseudo-label, and thus better performance. Or, whether the performance gain is minimal and the approximation objective is good as it is.

6. Also a follow-up: the authors consider uniform prior over the views. I wonder if one could be a bit more clever here, e.g., depending on the "persona" or the "strengths" of the current LLM, one could take that into account to make the prior non-uniform?

7. (Minor) As in many infomax papers (and as a theoretician myself), I wonder if this formulation of infomax (and its approximation) has been theoretically studied before, i.e., whether prior generalization bounds are applicable here (e.g., [3]). Or does this warrant further investigation for future work? If yes, which part of the new formulation yields novelty compared to prior literature?

8. (Minor) Very recently, there have been some issues regarding floating-point operations (https://x.com/QPHutu/status/1984258808332550245). Can the authors comment on whether this issue(?) applies to their experiments?
